title: The Allure of Abandoned Places
instructions: For questions 1-8, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
passage:
There is a peculiar thrill in trespass, and nowhere is this more (1)___ than among the growing community of urban explorers who seek out derelict factories, disused asylums and crumbling grand hotels. Clutching torches and cameras rather than crowbars, these self-styled custodians of decay insist that their motives are more reverent than reckless.

Critics, understandably wary of trespass law and the risk of injury, (2)___ the romance of ruin as little more than aestheticised rubbernecking - a voyeuristic thrill dressed up in the language of heritage. Yet the impulse itself is far from new: eighteenth-century aristocrats went to considerable (3)___ to have artificial ruins built on their estates, purely so they might (4)___ on the passage of time from a tastefully overgrown folly.

What has changed is the audience. Photographs that once circulated among a handful of connoisseurs now (5)___ across social media within minutes, turning once-obscure buildings into pilgrimage sites and, inevitably, (6)___ the very decay that made them alluring in the first place, as footfall, graffiti and souvenir-hunting take their toll.

Some explorers have therefore grown quietly (7)___ about sharing locations at all, preferring to let a building's mystique outlive its anonymity rather than (8)___ it to an audience that may trample straight through the very atmosphere it came to admire.

questions.explanation: 'More pronounced' means more noticeable or evident. The other options all involve formally stating something aloud, which doesn't fit 'nowhere is this more ___'.

'Dismiss X as Y' is the fixed pattern for characterising something negatively. 'Resign' pairs with 'to' or 'from', 'discard' and 'relinquish' mean to get rid of/give up and don't take an 'as' complement here.
'Go to considerable lengths' is a fixed idiom meaning to make a great effort. 'Distance', 'extent' and 'measure' don't fit this verb pattern ('went to considerable ___ to have...built').
'Muse on' is a fixed phrasal verb meaning to reflect thoughtfully on something. 'Amuse', 'bemuse' and 'accuse' are unrelated in meaning and don't combine with 'on' in this sense.

'Ricochet across' vividly captures images bouncing rapidly and uncontrollably between users. 'Ripple' suggests a gentler, gradual spread; 'radiate' normally pairs with 'from' a source; 'resonate' describes emotional impact, not speed of spread.
The sentence describes an ironic, unwanted side effect of attention: it speeds up the very decay admirers came to see. 'Lessening', 'delaying' and 'halting' all contradict the word 'inevitably'.

'Reticent about' means unwilling to disclose information. The other three words share a similar sound/ending but mean, respectively, 'good at remembering', 'living somewhere' and 'echoing/full of meaning'.

'Surrender it to an audience' fits the idea of giving up a location's secrecy. 'Relegate' means to demote to a lower rank/category, 'subject...to' usually pairs with an ordeal or scrutiny rather than 'an audience', and 'commit' pairs with 'to memory/paper'.
